Hence the estimated lifetime, combined with the relatively low dust mass compared to protoplanetary discs (Figure 2), leads us to believe that at least some of the dust is secondary in nature.

If the gas was secondary, then based on the $\sim10^{-2}$ M$_{\oplus}$ CO gas mass upper limit, from our $^{13}$CO non-detection, it would be depleted on very short timescales, and replenishment at the required rate seems unlikely. This strongly suggests that at least the inner disc retains primordial, $H_2$-rich gas.
It is important to note that from the CO gas mass alone, of (1.62 ± 0.17) $\times$ 10$^{-4}$$M_{\oplus}$, it is impossible to fully rule out the secondary origin scenario.

all_quotes.quote: Both its stellar temperature and luminosity are inconsistent with the star being on the AGB. Moreover, there is no evidence to suggest that HD 44892 is a binary system, hence this scenario is inapplicable here.

If the alternative age of 800 Myr is considered, HD 44892 would be an outlier in terms of its dust mass (temperature-dependent), 12 $\mu$m excess, and CO gas mass, strongly suggesting that this is the case of a young pre-main sequence star.
This mass is highly dependent on the dust temperature, which is uncertain given the emission is only marginally resolved along the major axis.
